youtube.title: Vietnam's S Shape: 1,650 km Long, Only 50 km Wide at the Waist
youtube.description:
Why is Vietnam shaped like an S? The country runs about 1,650 km from the Chinese border to the Cà Mau cape, yet near Đồng Hới it is only about 50 km from the Lao border to the sea. That thin waist has decided where the country was split, how it is fed and what it argues about today.

On the map we measure the Annamite wall and the two rice deltas, then follow the lines drawn from 938 to 1976: the southward advance into Champa and the Mekong, the Trịnh–Nguyễn border at the Gianh River, French Indochina and the 17th parallel. Then the rivalry at sea and up the Mekong, with each side's case in its own terms, and three things that could change the S: a sinking delta, a high-speed railway and the contested islands.

{CHAPTERS}

sources.claim: At its narrowest, Vietnam is about 50 kilometres from the mountains to the sea
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vietnam' (online edition, accessed November 2026): less than 50 km wide at its narrowest, in the central region

sources.claim: Vietnam runs some 1,650 kilometres from the Chinese border to Cà Mau
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vietnam' (accessed November 2026)

sources.claim: More than 100 million people live in Vietnam
sources.source: General Statistics Office of Vietnam, average population 2024, socio-economic report (January 2025)

sources.claim: Phones and footwear are among goods leaving Vietnam
sources.source: General Statistics Office of Vietnam, 2024 exports by commodity (January 2025): phones and components, footwear among the largest export groups

sources.claim: In 1069 the Lý dynasty took three Cham districts around today's Đồng Hới
sources.source: K. W. Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (Cambridge University Press, 2013)

sources.claim: The thinnest stretch lies near the city of Đồng Hới
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vietnam' (narrowest in the central region); Quảng Bình provincial government portal, province profile

sources.claim: At that waist the country is roughly thirty-three times longer than it is wide
sources.source: Arithmetic from Britannica's figures: 1,650 km ÷ 50 km

sources.claim: Land borders run about 4,600 kilometres; the border with Laos is some 2,160 kilometres
sources.source: CIA World Factbook, 'Vietnam' (accessed November 2026): total 4,616 km; Laos 2,161 km, China 1,297 km, Cambodia 1,158 km

sources.claim: Vietnam's government counts 3,260 kilometres of mainland coast
sources.source: Government of Vietnam / Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment, official coastline figure (more than 3,260 km, excluding islands)

sources.claim: The CIA World Factbook lists 3,444 kilometres of coastline
sources.source: CIA World Factbook, 'Vietnam', coastline (accessed November 2026)

sources.claim: The Annamite Range runs roughly 1,100 kilometres
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Annamese Cordillera' (accessed November 2026)

sources.claim: For long stretches the border with Laos follows the Annamite heights; the centre is a chain of narrow coastal plains cut by short, steep rivers
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vietnam', Land and Relief sections (accessed November 2026)

sources.claim: Vietnamese often picture their country as a carrying pole with a basket of rice at each end
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vietnam' (accessed November 2026)

sources.claim: The Red River Delta covers about 15,000 square kilometres
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Red River' (accessed November 2026)

sources.claim: The Mekong Delta covers about 40,000 square kilometres
sources.source: General Statistics Office of Vietnam, Statistical Yearbook, land area of the Mekong River Delta region

sources.claim: The Mekong Delta harvested about 24 million tonnes of rice in 2023, more than half of the national crop
sources.source: General Statistics Office of Vietnam, Statistical Yearbook 2023: paddy output by region (Mekong Delta about 24.3 of 43.5 million tonnes)

sources.claim: In 2024 rice exports reached a record of about nine million tonnes
sources.source: General Statistics Office of Vietnam and Vietnam Customs, annual trade reports 2020–2024 (2024: about 9.18 million tonnes, about US$5.75 billion)

sources.claim: National Route 1 and one railway, finished by the French in 1936, link the two deltas
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vietnam', Transportation; Vietnam Railways (VNR), history of the North–South line

sources.claim: The railway is about 1,726 kilometres long and the fastest passenger trains take more than 30 hours
sources.source: Vietnam Railways (VNR), Hanoi–Saigon line length and SE-series timetables (2026)

sources.claim: Chinese dynasties ruled the delta for most of the thousand years after the Han conquest of 111 BCE
sources.source: K. W. Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vietnam', History

sources.claim: In 938 Ngô Quyền defeated a Southern Han fleet at the mouth of the Bạch Đằng River, using iron-tipped stakes hidden by the tide
sources.source: K. W. Taylor, The Birth of Vietnam (University of California Press, 1983); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ngo Quyen'

sources.claim: The northern line was fixed by a Sino-French convention in 1887 and a new treaty in 1999
sources.source: Sino-French Convention on the delimitation of the frontier, 26 June 1887; Land Border Treaty between Vietnam and China, signed 30 December 1999

sources.claim: Champa was a chain of kingdoms along the central coast with its own ports, temples and script
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Champa' (accessed November 2026)

sources.claim: Mỹ Sơn has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999
sources.source: UNESCO World Heritage List, 'My Son Sanctuary', inscribed 1999

sources.claim: In 1306 two districts around Huế were exchanged for Princess Huyền Trân's marriage to the Cham king
sources.source: K. W. Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

sources.claim: In 1471 the armies of Lê Thánh Tông took the Cham capital of Vijaya, near today's Quy Nhơn
sources.source: K. W. Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Champa'

sources.claim: The southward advance, Nam tiến, ran for more than seven centuries (1069–1832)
sources.source: K. W. Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

sources.claim: From 1627 the Trịnh and Nguyễn lords fought seven campaigns; the Nguyễn built earthen walls near Đồng Hới
sources.source: K. W. Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013); Li Tana, Nguyễn Cochinchina (Cornell SEAP, 1998)

sources.claim: After 1672 the Gianh River served as a border for roughly a hundred years
sources.source: Li Tana, Nguyễn Cochinchina (1998); K. W. Taylor (2013)

sources.claim: In 1698 Nguyễn Hữu Cảnh set up a Vietnamese administration at Gia Định, the town that became Saigon
sources.source: K. W. Taylor (2013); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ho Chi Minh City'

sources.claim: Cambodians call the delta Kampuchea Krom; Saigon's old Khmer name was Prey Nokor
sources.source: David Chandler, A History of Cambodia (4th ed., Westview, 2008); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ho Chi Minh City'

sources.claim: In 1832 Emperor Minh Mạng abolished the last Cham principality, around Phan Rang
sources.source: K. W. Taylor (2013); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Champa'

sources.claim: France took southern provinces by treaty in 1862 and 1867 and made the rest a protectorate in 1884
sources.source: Treaty of Saigon, 5 June 1862; French annexation of western Cochinchina, 1867; Treaty of Huế, 6 June 1884; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'French Indochina'

sources.claim: In 1887 France grouped its colonies as French Indochina; Laos was added after a treaty with Siam in 1893
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'French Indochina'; Franco-Siamese Treaty, 3 October 1893

sources.claim: Lines between Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia were drawn as internal French administrative boundaries
sources.source: Martin Stuart-Fox, A History of Laos (Cambridge University Press, 1997)

sources.claim: In July 1954 the Geneva Accords set a provisional line near the 17th parallel, along the Bến Hải River, with a demilitarised zone up to five kilometres on either side
sources.source: Agreement on the Cessation of Hostilities in Viet-Nam, Geneva, 20 July 1954, Article 1

sources.claim: The 1954 line ran about 70 kilometres south of Đồng Hới
sources.source: Straight-line map measurement, Đồng Hới to Hiền Lương bridge on the Bến Hải River

sources.claim: Wartime supply routes ran through Laos and Cambodia along the Ho Chi Minh Trail
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ho Chi Minh Trail'

sources.claim: The country was formally reunified in July 1976
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Vietnam': reunification proclaimed 2 July 1976

sources.claim: A coast can claim an exclusive economic zone of 200 nautical miles under the 1982 convention
sources.source: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (1982), Article 57

sources.claim: China has held the Paracel Islands since January 1974; Vietnam and Taiwan also claim them
sources.source: CIA World Factbook, 'Paracel Islands' (accessed November 2026)

sources.claim: China, Taiwan and Vietnam claim all the Spratlys; the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei claim parts
sources.source: CIA World Factbook, 'Spratly Islands' (accessed November 2026)

sources.claim: Vietnam holds more Spratly features than any other claimant
sources.source: CSIS Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, Island Tracker and Vietnam reclamation reports (2024)

sources.claim: China and Vietnam have enlarged reefs with dredged sand, adding harbours, buildings and runways
sources.source: CSIS Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, reports 2015–2024

sources.claim: In 2016 a tribunal, in a case brought by the Philippines, rejected China's claim to historic rights inside the line
sources.source: Permanent Court of Arbitration, Case 2013-19, Award of 12 July 2016, and PCA press release of the same date

sources.claim: Beijing called the award null and void, with no binding force
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the People's Republic of China, statement of 12 July 2016

sources.claim: China says Chinese sailors named and used these islands long before modern sea law
sources.source: State Council Information Office of China, white paper 'China Adheres to the Position of Settling Through Negotiation the Relevant Disputes Between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea', 13 July 2016

sources.claim: A Chinese government map first drew a dashed line around the sea in the late 1940s
sources.source: US Department of State, Limits in the Seas No. 143, 'China: Maritime Claims in the South China Sea' (December 2014)

sources.claim: Vietnam cites Nguyễn-era records of royal crews sent to the Paracels
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Vietnam, white papers on Hoàng Sa and Trường Sa (1979, 1981, 1988)

sources.claim: In May 2014 China placed an oil rig near the Paracels, in waters Vietnam claims, and it stayed ten weeks
sources.source: Reuters and The New York Times reporting, 2 May–15 July 2014; CSIS Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative

sources.claim: Vietnam's 2019 defence white paper sets out four noes, including no military alliances and no foreign bases
sources.source: Ministry of National Defence of Vietnam, 2019 Viet Nam National Defence (November 2019)

sources.claim: In 2024 Vietnam's biggest supplier was China and its biggest customer the United States
sources.source: General Statistics Office of Vietnam, 2024 trade report (January 2025): imports from China about US$144 billion, exports to the US about US$119.5 billion

sources.claim: The US Census Bureau puts the 2024 goods gap with Vietnam at 123.5 billion dollars
sources.source: US Census Bureau, Trade in Goods with Vietnam, 2024

sources.claim: Vietnam's statistics office puts the 2024 surplus with the US at 104.6 billion dollars
sources.source: General Statistics Office of Vietnam, 2024 trade report (January 2025)

sources.claim: The Mekong passes China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand and Cambodia before reaching Vietnam
sources.source: Mekong River Commission, basin overview

sources.claim: China has built 11 dams on the river's upper main stem
sources.source: Stimson Center, Mekong Dam Monitor (accessed November 2026)

sources.claim: Critics say the dams trap water and sediment; China says they release water in dry seasons and ease floods
sources.source: Stimson Center, Mekong Dam Monitor reports; Ministry of Foreign Affairs of China and Lancang-Mekong Cooperation statements (2020–2024)

sources.claim: In August 2024 Cambodia broke ground on the Funan Techo canal, some 180 kilometres from Phnom Penh to Kep
sources.source: Royal Government of Cambodia, groundbreaking 5 August 2024; Reuters, 5 August 2024

sources.claim: Vietnam has asked for data on the canal's effect; Cambodia says it draws little water and is its sovereign project
sources.source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Vietnam, spokesperson statements (2024); statements by Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet (2024)

sources.claim: A 2019 study in Nature Communications found the Mekong Delta stands on average just 0.8 metres above sea level
sources.source: Minderhoud et al., 'Mekong delta much lower than previously assumed in sea-level rise impact assessments', Nature Communications 10, 3847 (2019)

sources.claim: Groundwater pumping lowers parts of the delta a centimetre or more yearly
sources.source: Minderhoud et al., Environmental Research Letters 12, 064006 (2017)

sources.claim: In the dry seasons of 2016 and 2020 salt water pushed far up the delta's rivers into rice fields
sources.source: Mekong River Commission drought and salinity reports (2016, 2020); Government of Vietnam emergency declarations in Mekong Delta provinces (2020)

sources.claim: In November 2024 the National Assembly approved a 1,541-kilometre high-speed line for trains of up to 350 km/h, costing about 67 billion dollars, targeted for 2035
sources.source: National Assembly of Vietnam, Resolution 172/2024/QH15, 30 November 2024

sources.claim: Supporters say it would tie the narrow middle to both ends; critics have asked whether its cost can be repaid
sources.source: National Assembly debate on the North–South high-speed railway, November 2024, reported by VnExpress International

sources.claim: Washington set a 20 percent tariff on Vietnamese goods in July 2025
sources.source: The White House, Executive Order 14326, 'Further Modifying the Reciprocal Tariff Rates', 31 July 2025, Annex I

sources.claim: Chile is about 4,300 kilometres long and on average 177 kilometres wide
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chile' (accessed November 2026)
